unmapped_findings: At 900 °C and above, the ferrite (α) phase of the Ni-containing Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni alloy contains nano-sized disc-like B2 particles of Ni-Al type (vs Fe-Al type in Ni-free samples); the discs are of Ni-Al type in the Ni-containing samples.

The nanoindentation technique used cannot measure the hardness of isolated nano-sized precipitates; it measures instead the hardness of the nano-sized features within a surrounding matrix, giving a compound (matrix + particle) hardness value.

According to the Orowan mechanism the increase in shear stress Δτ is proportional to the inverse of the precipitates' diameter (Δτ ∝ R^−1.25); the higher hardness at higher annealing temperatures is attributed to the uniformly distributed nano-sized disc-like B2 particles that increase the shear resistance of the α-matrix.

The higher hardness of the Ni-containing B2 is attributed to the B2 composition being NiAl rather than FeAl, with Ni-Al bonds reported to be stronger than Fe-Al bonds; ab-initio literature values show Ni-Al compounds have larger elastic constants (C11 221.67→375.61 GPa and C44 116.99→133.21 GPa from NiAl to Ni3Al) than Fe-Al compounds.

Increasing the annealing temperature increases the Ni content of the B2 particles: the coarse NiAl-type B2 particles in the γ phase of the Ni-containing sample increase in hardness from 9.1 GPa (Ni: 8.2 wt.%) at 500 °C to 10.5 GPa (Ni: 10.1 wt.%) at 1050 °C.

Calculated elastic constants (Table 3) were related to the experimental hardness: the insertion of a C atom only enhances the elastic constant of the κ-phase (L1'2), while Mn substitution (Fe3AlC → Mn3AlC) increases the elastic constants, confirming the experimental increase in hardness of κ enriched in Mn.
